tldr: By just taking a single video scanning around a static object with a smartphone or similar device, RORA builds simulation-ready assets combining photorealistic appearance (3DGS), physically interactive meshes, and accurate joint kinematics (URDF) using automatic suggestions and minimal manual adjustments.
hero_caption: Overall concept of RORA. From just a single static object video, it outputs articulated assets that integrate meshes for physical interaction and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) for visual reproduction, enabling immediate robot manipulation execution in Isaac Sim and Unreal Engine.
overview:
In robot learning, "Real-to-Sim"—faithfully replicating real-world environments inside simulators—is a crucial approach for closing the sim-to-real gap. In recent years, the emergence of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has enabled extremely high-fidelity visual reproduction. However, bringing "articulated objects" with internal joints—such as drawers, spray bottles, and tools—into simulation environments has remained a very high hurdle.

Existing articulation estimation methods either required humans to scan multiple states while manually moving the object, or relied on the common-sense reasoning of large vision-language models (VLMs) to infer joints. However, the former involves extremely tedious data collection and struggles with complex multi-joint kinematics (linked structures), while the latter fails on unseen geometries and intricate mechanisms.

To address this, the authors propose "RORA," a framework that takes only a "single video scan" of a static object as input and automatically calculates and presents candidate joint axes from the local boundary geometry of the object. By combining convex decomposition, intuitive human grouping of parts, and an automatic joint suggestion algorithm based on geometric analysis of boundary loops, even complex multi-joint and multi-link mechanisms can be accurately modeled with just tens of seconds of GUI interaction.

In experiments, the method was evaluated on the PartNet-Mobility benchmark and various real-world daily objects, demonstrating that it achieves extremely high geometric and visual accuracy even on complex kinematic structures where existing methods completely fail. Furthermore, the authors imported the created assets into NVIDIA Isaac Sim and Unreal Engine 5, demonstrating real-time teleoperation and dexterous interaction with five-finger hands and humanoid robots.
contributions: Established an end-to-end pipeline capable of reconstructing articulated assets from a single static video scan without capturing dynamic object manipulation.

Accurately recovered complex kinematics such as branching structures (1-to-N) and multi-link chains through the fusion of local boundary geometric feature analysis and lightweight human-in-the-loop (HIL).

Bound convex mesh structures for physics simulation and 3DGS for real-time photorealistic rendering on a part-by-part basis, outputting a hybrid representation immediately deployable to simulators as URDF.

sections.heading: Why Do We Need to Create "Moving Objects" from Static Videos?
sections.summary: Building photorealistic simulation environments is essential for robot sim-to-real transfer, but reproducing articulated objects with joints has been difficult. This paper proposes "RORA," a semi-automatic pipeline that generates high-precision articulated assets from a single static object video.
sections.details:
In manipulation learning for robots such as humanoids, how effectively one can close the visual and physical difference between simulation and the real world (the sim-to-real gap) determines success. Recently, research using 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to render real-world scenes directly inside simulators has become active, but most of those works focused on "rigid bodies" (non-moving, monolithic objects). However, many objects we encounter in daily life possess internal kinematics, such as hinges and sliding mechanisms.

Prior works for creating articulated models from real objects generally fall into two categories. One is the approach of letting VLMs infer joint types and locations, and the other is tracking dynamic motions by scanning the object moving across multiple states to reverse-engineer constraints. However, VLMs are susceptible to training data bias and easily fail on complex multi-joints, while motion tracking methods require the labor-intensive chore of "humans manually scanning while manipulating joints repeatedly."

"RORA (Realistic Object Reconstruction with Articulation)," proposed in this work, takes only a single video captured around a static object as input. By geometrically calculating candidate joint axes from the local boundary geometry of the object and adopting a suggestion-based human-in-the-loop (HIL) workflow where users click to choose in a GUI, it minimizes manual burden while accurately recovering branching structures and parent-child multi-link (serial chain) mechanisms. The output is a URDF format where collision meshes and photorealistic 3DGS work in tandem, ready for immediate import into robot simulators.

captions.F2: Overall pipeline of RORA. It consists of six stages: initial reconstruction, mesh repair, convex decomposition, user part merging, geometry-based joint suggestion and selection, and URDF export for simulation.

sections.heading: How Did Prior Works Tackle This, and Where Did They Get Stuck?
sections.summary: We review three streams of research: photorealistic representation with 3DGS, motion-based articulation estimation, and deep learning/VLM-based articulation methods. All had issues with operational cost or generalization to multi-joint systems.
sections.details:
Related works can be categorized into three main areas:

- **Gaussian–Mesh Hybrid Reconstruction**
3DGS has rapidly become popular as a high-quality spatial representation and is utilized in robotics, such as in RE3SIM, RialTo, and SplatSim, to close visual sim-to-real gaps. However, most of these treat an object as a single static rigid mesh, making it impossible to articulate internal joints and interact part by part.

- **Motion-Based Articulation**
These methods observe an object's deformation or motion to reverse-engineer joint constraints. Approaches such as PARIS (estimating a single joint from 2-state RGB images), PARIS* and DTA (handling multiple joints with RGB-D cameras), and ScrewSplat (jointly optimizing screw theory and 3DGS from multi-state RGB images) have been proposed. However, these require users to manually manipulate object joints and scan multiple times, presenting a major practical bottleneck. Moreover, in multi-link structures where moving one joint alters the position of the next, trajectories become complicated and tracking frequently fails.

- **VLM and Learning-Based Articulation**
Examples include Articulate-Anything, which assigns joints from CAD libraries via a VLM agent loop, and URDFormer, which directly regresses part shapes and URDFs from a single image using a ViT. While appealing due to being fully automatic, they rely heavily on the training dataset distribution; on out-of-distribution (OOD) diverse real-world daily objects, link placement mistakes and misidentified joint axes occur frequently.

RORA elegantly resolves both the "burden of dynamic motion scanning" and the "out-of-distribution errors of learned models" by combining a joint suggestion algorithm based on local boundary geometry with minimal human feedback.

sections.heading: The 6-Stage Pipeline of RORA: Extracting Joint Axes from Local Geometry
sections.summary: Meshes generated from video are convexly decomposed, and users merge them into meaningful parts. Then, candidate joint axes are geometrically computed from contact boundary loops between parts using SVM and EM, and exported as a URDF.
sections.details:
RORA processes data through the following six stages:

### 1. Initial Reconstruction & Refinement
First, GS2Mesh is used to recover 3DGS and an initial mesh from a single video. SAM2 segments the target object, and visibility count thresholding extracts only the 3D Gaussians belonging to the object. Because occlusion creates holes and floating noise on the bottom of the initial mesh, Principal Component Analysis (PCA) finds the bottom surface normal to align it upright along the Z-axis, followed by hole filling to repair it into a watertight mesh.

### 2. Decomposition & Segmentation
Based on the assumption that articulated sub-parts have geometrically salient shapes, the Approximate Convex Decomposition (ACD) algorithm (CoACD) splits the mesh into numerous convex polygon pieces. Since automatic segmentation based on similar textures is prone to errors, a lightweight HIL step is performed where the user simply assigns group numbers (part IDs) to convex pieces in a GUI. Unassigned vertices are merged into the nearest group via $L_2$ distance. Furthermore, each 3D Gaussian point is bound to its corresponding mesh part via k-nearest neighbor (KNN) majority voting.

### 3. Automatic Joint Suggestion Algorithm
This is the technical core of the paper. Joint axes are derived geometrically through four steps: boundary detection, axis estimation, bidirectional fusion, and candidate proposal.
- **Boundary Detection**: A graph is built from boundary vertices where part $i$ is adjacent to another part $j$, and closed loops (boundary cycles) are enumerated using Depth-First Search (DFS).
- **Axis Estimation**: For each boundary cycle, a linear SVM is fitted to planar shapes to find the normal vector $\bm{n}$. For non-planar shapes like corners, the EM algorithm fits two hyperplanes to find their intersection line vector $\bm{x}$.
- **Bidirectional Fusion**: Connections from part $i$ to $j$ and from $j$ to $i$ are paired and averaged to generate three candidate vectors: the normal $\bm{n}$, the intersection line $\bm{x}$, and their cross product $\bm{p} = \bm{n} \times \bm{x}$.
- **Joint Candidate Proposal**: When multiple contact boundaries exist between parts (for example, a toolbox handle supported at two points), the midpoint of the connection origins and the line connecting them are automatically added as an additional joint candidate.

### 4. Export Stage
The user clicks the correct joint axis among the candidates suggested in the GUI and specifies the joint type (revolute, prismatic, or fixed). With just this, a URDF completely describing the object's kinematics and hybrid assets linking 3DGS and meshes to each link are exported.

captions.F3: Flow of the automatic joint suggestion algorithm. It extracts part boundary cycles and estimates normal and intersection vectors using SVM and EM. By fusing bidirectional connections and adding the cross-product vector, three axes are proposed as joint candidates.
captions.F4: Example of joint candidate generation when multiple boundaries exist. When there are two contact points, such as between Part 1 (body) and Part 5 (handle), the axis connecting the two connection centers is cleverly suggested as an additional revolute axis candidate.

sections.heading: Demonstrating Overwhelming Accuracy Even on Complex Multi-Joints Where Existing Methods Fail
sections.summary: Evaluations were conducted on the PartNet-Mobility dataset and real objects. While VLM-based and motion-tracking baselines broke down on multi-joint and multi-link objects, RORA achieved overwhelming geometric and visual accuracy, and demonstrated teleoperation in physics simulators.
sections.details:
### Benchmark Quantitative Evaluation
Using the PartNet-Mobility dataset, RORA was compared against state-of-the-art baselines: "Articulate-Anything (AA: VLM-based, internal model Gemini-2.5-Flash)" and "ScrewSplat (motion-tracking-based)." While baselines require dynamic object motion videos (15 seconds) or 240 multi-view images across five articulated states, RORA takes only 48 images of a single static state as input. Evaluations were conducted across difficulty levels: single joint (Cat I: 6 types), multiple joints (Cat II: 6 types), and multi-link chains (Cat III: 4 types).

- **Geometric Accuracy (Table I)**: While all methods performed reasonably well on single joints (Cat I), the baselines suffered catastrophic performance drops on complex multiple joints (Cat II) and Cat III where child links move in tandem with parent links. AA matched incorrect CAD models due to VLM reasoning errors, and ScrewSplat failed to track coupled non-linear motions. In contrast, RORA made virtually no joint type errors even on Cat III thanks to geometry-based suggestions and human selection, recording the lowest errors in both angle and position.
- **Visual Fidelity (Table II, Fig. 5)**: In rendering quality (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) with joints articulated, RORA consistently earned the highest scores across all categories. Because baselines had misaligned joint axes, their appearance broke down significantly when articulated.
- **Processing Time (Table III)**: Although one might expect HIL to take long, RORA's total processing time averaged 7 minutes 23 seconds, of which human interaction accounted for only 42 seconds. AA's duration fluctuated due to waiting for iterative VLM reasoning, and ScrewSplat required 6 minutes 56 seconds of optimization on average; thus RORA achieves overwhelmingly higher quality in roughly comparable time.

### Real-World Object Scans and Robot Manipulation in Simulation
Real-world laptops, desk lamps, toolboxes, spray bottles, fire extinguishers, and Wi-Fi routers were captured and converted into assets (Fig. 6). Accurate joint motions were reproduced while beautifully preserving label text and fine textures.

Furthermore, to demonstrate practical utility, teleoperation was conducted in the Unreal Engine 5.3-based HERMES simulator with a 5-finger hand (Inspire Hand) pulling a spray trigger and rotating a coffee grinder handle. Additionally, a Fourier GR-1 humanoid was controlled via Meta Quest in NVIDIA Isaac Sim to intuitively adjust a desk lamp arm (Fig. 7). Stable physical contact computation via meshes and beautiful rendering via 3DGS were confirmed to work seamlessly together.

captions.F5: Rendering comparison on PartNet-Mobility. When transitioning from the zero joint position (left) to an articulated state (right), baselines (AA, SCREW) suffer from missing parts or collapse, whereas the proposed method (OURS) maintains quality indistinguishable from ground truth (GT).
captions.F6: Qualitative comparison on real-world objects. It shows that complex joint axes in real environments (yellow arrows), such as laptops, multi-joint desk lamps, and router antennas, are reconstructed accurately.
captions.F7: Manipulation demonstrations in simulator environments. The top row shows spray triggering and coffee grinding in Unreal Engine, while the bottom row shows desk lamp manipulation by the GR-1 humanoid in Isaac Sim.

sections.heading: Summary and Future Outlook: Unleashing Real-World Tools into Simulators
sections.summary: RORA was proposed to rapidly generate articulated assets integrating 3DGS and meshes from a single static video. Future plans include overcoming transparent and reflective objects, verifying sim-to-real transfer with humanoids, and building an asset-sharing platform for the community.
sections.details:
In this paper, the authors presented "RORA," a semi-automatic pipeline that reconstructs simulation-ready articulated assets from a single video capturing a static object. By incorporating minimal human-in-the-loop interaction—intuitive part grouping and geometry-based automatic joint axis suggestions—it completely overcomes the breakdown on multi-joint and multi-link structures seen in prior fully automatic methods. The generated assets integrate seamlessly into Isaac Sim and Unreal Engine, serving as an extremely valuable environment for training and data collection for advanced dexterous robot manipulation.

On the other hand, limitations remain in the current framework:
- **Tiny Parts and Non-Salient Geometries**: Because it relies on convex decomposition and geometric boundary analysis, it may fail to isolate components that are extremely small relative to the overall object, or parts that do not protrude geometrically from the surface.
- **Weakness on Reflective and Transparent Materials**: Inheriting common challenges of 3DGS and initial mesh generation, reconstructing transparent objects like glass or metal surfaces with strong specular reflections remains difficult.

The authors plan to train humanoid robots using assets built with RORA to verify improvements in sim-to-real success rates in the physical world. Additionally, they plan to release a platform to share and distribute reconstructed high-quality assets to the broader community.

takeaways: Abandoning the conventional notion of "scanning moving objects" and reverse-calculating joint axes from static contact boundary geometry (normals and intersection lines via SVM and EM) is an exceptionally powerful paradigm shift.

Rather than clinging to full automation and suffering from VLM hallucinations, inserting a lightweight suggestion-based HIL step (~42 seconds of single-click selections) dramatically enhances engineering reliability and practicality.

The hybrid design binding collision convex meshes (URDF) and high-fidelity rendering 3DGS on a per-part basis could become the standard for building sim-to-real robot learning environments going forward.
limitations: Parts whose movable sections do not protrude geometrically (e.g., embedded flush on the same plane) or are too small relative to the whole object cannot be separated by convex decomposition.
Because it inherits the limitations of 3DGS itself, geometric reconstruction easily fails on transparent glass or surfaces with strong gloss and specular reflections.
